title: Social Engineering & the Human Factor
summary: Attackers usually find it cheaper to manipulate a person than to break a system. Learn the anatomy of phishing, vishing, pretexting, and business email compromise, and why awareness training is a real control, not a formality.

slides.markdown:
Ask a red teamer for the fastest way into a hardened company and the answer is almost never a zero-day — it's an email. **Social engineering** attacks the person operating the system instead of the system itself, and it works because humans are built to trust, help, and comply with authority — properties no firewall patches away.

This topic covers the attack families you'll be asked to recognize — phishing, vishing, pretexting, business email compromise — plus the uncomfortable fact that technical controls alone can't close this gap. Verizon's Data Breach Investigations Report has put a human element in the majority of breaches for years running, which is why every serious security program treats people as a layer to defend, not a weakness to lecture at.

slides.sectionTitle: Why humans are the most-targeted layer
slides.markdown:
Attackers go after people because the cost-benefit is unbeatable: breaking modern cryptography or a hardened, patched server takes real skill and time. Getting one employee to click a link takes a well-written email and five minutes.

The psychological levers are consistent across almost every social engineering attack, and worth naming explicitly because they're what you're actually defending against:

- **Authority** — a message that appears to come from the CEO, IT, or a regulator gets less scrutiny.
- **Urgency** — "act in the next 10 minutes or your account is locked" short-circuits careful thinking.
- **Fear** — a threat of consequences (account suspension, legal action) pushes people to comply first, verify later.
- **Helpfulness** — most people default to being helpful to a colleague or a plausible stranger, and attackers exploit exactly that default.

No access control, encryption, or firewall rule changes any of these — which is why this topic sits in Security Fundamentals rather than under a specific technical control.

slides.sectionTitle: Phishing: the anatomy of a convincing email
slides.markdown:
**Phishing** is a mass, untargeted email attack designed to harvest credentials or deliver malware by impersonating a trusted sender. A convincing one is built from a small, repeatable set of parts:

- **A plausible sender** — a spoofed or lookalike domain (`paypa1.com`, or a display name of "IT Support" over a random address).
- **A believable pretext** — a password expiry notice, an invoice, a shared document link — something the target has a real reason to expect.
- **Urgency or a benefit** — act now or lose access; or claim a reward.
- **A single call to action** — one link or one attachment, minimizing the target's decision points.
- **A landing page that mimics the real login** pixel-for-pixel, harvesting the credential the moment it's typed.

The defense that scales best isn't "train people to spot bad grammar" — modern phishing is often grammatically perfect. It's **verify the sender through a second channel** before acting on anything urgent or financial, and **hover before you click** to see the real destination URL, not the display text.

slides.subTitle: Targeted variants
slides.markdown:
Generic phishing is a numbers game — send a million emails, a small percentage clicks. **Spear phishing** trades volume for research: the attacker studies a specific target (their employer, their manager's name, a recent project from LinkedIn) and writes an email that fits their exact context, which pushes click-through rates far higher.

**Whaling** is spear phishing aimed specifically at executives or other high-value targets — a CFO, a general counsel — because their access and authority make a single successful compromise worth disproportionately more.

The research effort is what makes these dangerous: a spear-phishing email referencing a real vendor, a real project name, and a colleague's real name doesn't trigger the same suspicion generic phishing does. This is also why oversharing on LinkedIn and public conference bios is a real security concern — it's reconnaissance material handed over for free, and it's exactly what feeds business email compromise, covered shortly.

slides.subTitle: Phone- and SMS-based social engineering
slides.markdown:
The same manipulation, different channel — chosen because phone and text bypass the spam filters and link-scanning tools that now catch a lot of email phishing.

- **Vishing (voice phishing)** — a phone call impersonating IT support, a bank's fraud department, or an executive's assistant, asking the target to read out a one-time code, reset a password, or approve a push notification. Voice cloning has made this sharply more dangerous: a cloned voice of a real executive asking a finance team to "confirm" a wire transfer has caused real financial losses.
- **Smishing (SMS phishing)** — a text claiming a package delivery failed, a bank flagged a transaction, or an account needs re-verification, with a malicious link. It works partly because people apply less scrutiny to texts than to email, and mobile browsers make a spoofed URL harder to inspect.

Both exploit the same urgency-plus-authority pattern as email phishing — the channel changes, the psychology doesn't.

**Pretexting** is inventing a plausible scenario to justify an unusual request — the fabricated context that makes the ask feel reasonable rather than suspicious.

Classic examples: an attacker calls IT support claiming to be a traveling employee locked out of their account, and asks for a password reset. Or someone in a delivery uniform tells a receptionist they're here to "service the server room" and gets waved through — this is impersonation with a physical pretext, sometimes called **tailgating** when it's about following an authorized person through a locked door.

What makes pretexting effective is that the request itself is often something a legitimate employee asks for all the time — a password reset, a badge swipe, a document. The social engineering isn't in the ask, it's in the fabricated identity and urgency wrapped around it. This is exactly why **verifying identity through an independent channel** (call the employee back on a known number, don't just trust caller ID) is the control that actually generalizes across every pretexting variant.

slides.subTitle: Social engineering with a wire transfer at the end
slides.markdown:
**Business email compromise (BEC)** is the financially costliest form of social engineering, and the FBI's IC3 has consistently ranked it as the single largest category of reported cybercrime losses, ahead of ransomware.

The playbook: an attacker either spoofs or actually compromises an executive's email account, then emails someone in finance with an urgent, plausible request — "wire $80,000 to this new vendor account today, I'm in a meeting and can't call." No malware, no exploit, no technical breach required. The entire attack is one well-timed, well-researched email.

What makes BEC hard to stop with technical controls alone: the request looks completely normal to an email filter — it's not a malicious link or attachment, just text asking for a routine-seeming action. The control that actually works is **procedural**: mandatory out-of-band verification (a phone call to a known number) for any wire transfer or vendor payment change, regardless of how urgent or how senior the requester appears.

slides.sectionTitle: A phishing attack chain, end to end
slides.markdown:
![A five-stage phishing attack chain from spoofed email to lateral movement, with the control that breaks each stage](assets/phishing-attack-chain.svg)

The reason to look at the whole chain rather than just "the click": every stage is a separate place a defense can intervene, and no single control covers all five. Email filtering can catch stage 1 before it lands. Awareness training reduces the odds of stage 2. **MFA is the single highest-leverage control here** — even with a correct, harvested password, stage 4 fails without the second factor.

This is why "train users not to click links" alone is a weak defense-in-depth story: it's one control at one stage, and it's the stage most dependent on human judgment holding up every single time.

slides.subTitle: Why you need both
slides.markdown:
| | Technical controls (MFA, allowlists, email filtering) | Awareness training |
|---|---|---|
| **What it stops** | The consequence, even after a click (MFA blocks login without the second factor) | The click itself, by teaching recognition |
| **Scales with headcount** | Yes — one policy protects everyone equally | Partially — training decays, needs repetition |
| **Fails against** | Push-notification fatigue, SIM-swapped MFA, allowlist gaps for new domains | A sufficiently well-researched, novel pretext that doesn't match training examples |
| **Cost to run** | Mostly upfront engineering + minor user friction | Ongoing — phishing simulations, refreshers |

Neither one is sufficient alone. Technical controls fail quietly against a novel enough pretext or a fatigued user who approves an MFA push without looking. Training fails against anyone having a bad, distracted, or rushed moment — and everyone has one eventually. Layer them: training reduces the click rate, MFA and out-of-band verification contain the damage when a click happens anyway.

slides.sectionTitle: "Our engineers would never fall for this"
slides.markdown:
A dangerous assumption: that technical staff are immune to social engineering because they understand how the attacks work.

They aren't, and the data backs this up — internal phishing simulations routinely show engineers, security staff, and even security *trainers* clicking at rates not far below the general population, especially on well-researched spear-phishing attempts. Understanding a concept intellectually doesn't stop it from working on you at 5pm on a Friday when you're tired, expecting an email, and it arrives at exactly the right moment.

The RSA breach in 2011 — a company whose entire business is security — started with a spear-phishing email opened by an employee. Twitter's 2020 high-profile account takeover started with a vishing call to employees who had legitimate admin access. Technical sophistication reduces susceptibility to generic, low-effort phishing; it does not make anyone immune to a well-crafted, well-timed pretext.

The implication: controls like MFA and out-of-band verification need to apply uniformly, including to the engineers and security staff who are most confident they'd never fall for it.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing an organization to resist it
slides.markdown:
The senior-level version of this topic isn't "don't click suspicious links" — it's designing processes that stay safe even when someone does.

What that looks like in practice:

- **No single-channel authorization for money or access.** Wire transfers, vendor bank-detail changes, and privilege escalations require out-of-band verification, full stop — no exception for urgency or seniority, because urgency and seniority are exactly what the attack impersonates.
- **MFA everywhere, phishing-resistant where it matters most** (hardware keys or platform authenticators over SMS codes, which are themselves phishable and SIM-swappable).
- **A fast, blame-free reporting path.** The single biggest lever against BEC and phishing isn't stopping the first click — it's how fast someone reports it, which determines whether the account gets locked in minutes or discovered in a breach report months later.
- **Simulated phishing as a metric, not a gotcha** — measuring click-through rate over time to see if training is working, not to punish individuals.

The common thread: assume a click will eventually happen to someone, and make sure the blast radius of that one click is small.
